newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece asks striking seamen to return to work.
newsitem.headline: Greece asks striking seamen to return to work.

text.p: Some Greek teachers on Monday launched work stoppages against tough incomes and tax policies while government spokesman Dimitris Reppas called on seamen to return to work after a court ruled that their strike is illegal.
High school teachers began an indefinite strike to press for better pay. Greece's biggest labour confederation, the GSEE, has announced a 24-hour nationwide walkout for Thursday.

Groups of workers have reacted strongly to Greece's 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, but technocrat Prime Minister Costas Simitis says bitter medicine is necessary for the country and has rejected all union demands.
The seamen's eight-day strike, affecting all ships with Greek crews, has kept most vessels idle at ports.
"They must consider the responsibilities for the social and political cost of the strike," the government spokesman told reporters.
The seamen's union has defied Friday's court ruling that declared their strike illegal and vowed to press on with their campaign for better pensions, insurance and tax treatment.
"We will continue the strike and we feel quite calm about it," said John Halas, secretary general of the Panhellenic Seamen's Federation.
Police said there were minor clashes in Patras on Monday when foreign truck drivers tried to force their way into ships destined for Italy but were blocked by seamen.
Civil aviation staff suspended stoppages that had crippled air transport in the past three days but threatened to resume the action if their economic demands were not met.
Farmers are threatening to resume blocking highways with tractors if demands for higher price supports, fuel and tax cuts are not met by February 4.
The GSEE is protesting against a new tax bill which abolishes a series of tax breaks for wage earners. The confederation also wants higher pensions for state pensioners and above-inflation pay rises.
The GSEE strike is expected to disrupt transport, state hospitals and public services. A number of state companies will be forces to operate with skeleton staffs.
